Daily deep-dive · Day 9

HyperLogLog

Count the number of distinct items in a billions-strong stream using ~12 KB of memory and one delightful trick: the rarest pattern you've seen tells you how much you've seen.

01The problem, in plain words

You want the count of distinct elements in a massive stream: unique visitors to a site, distinct search queries in a day, unique source IPs hitting a router. The obvious method — keep a hash set of everything seen and read its size — costs memory proportional to the number of distinct items. A billion uniques means storing a billion things.

HyperLogLog estimates that same count using a fixed, tiny footprint — about 12 KB — for cardinalities into the billions, with roughly 1% error. Twelve kilobytes to count billions of distinct things.

Analogy: a friend says, "I flipped a coin many times; the longest run of heads I ever got was 10 in a row." Roughly how many flips? A run of 10 heads is a 1-in-1024 event, so you'd guess they flipped on the order of 1000 times. You estimated the size of an effort from the rarity of its most extreme outcome — no need to have counted the flips.

02The core insight

the whole idea The rarest hash pattern you've observed is a proxy for how many distinct items you've hashed. Rare patterns only show up after many distinct tries.

Hash each item to a random-looking binary string, and count its leading zeros (the position of the leftmost 1). A hash starting 0001… has 3 leading zeros — a 1-in-16 pattern. Track the maximum leading-zero count ever seen: if the max is k, you've probably seen about 2^k distinct items, because such a pattern is a 1-in-2^(k+1) event.

Why it counts distinct items for free: hashing is deterministic, so the same item always yields the same hash and the same leading-zero count. Seeing "visitor A" a million times contributes exactly what seeing it once does. Duplicates change nothing.

03Killing the noise — many buckets

A single "max leading zeros" is wildly noisy: one freak hash starting with 20 zeros would blow the estimate to a million after only a handful of items. The fix is the statistician's standard move — run many independent estimators and combine them.

Use the first few bits of each hash to pick a bucket (register). 14 bits → 2¹⁴ = 16,384 buckets.
Use the remaining bits to compute the leading-zero count, and store the max in that bucket.
Each item updates exactly one bucket. Now you have thousands of independent estimators, each watching its own slice.
Combine all buckets and scale up to get the final distinct-count estimate.

04The two refinements that make it "Hyper"

Harmonic mean, not arithmetic mean. When fusing the buckets, HLL uses the harmonic mean, which heavily discounts large outliers — so one unlucky bucket that saw a freak 20-zero hash gets tamed instead of dominating. Swapping the plain average (the earlier "LogLog" algorithm) for the harmonic mean is precisely what put the "Hyper" in HyperLogLog and sharply improved accuracy.

A bias-correction constant. The raw formula is systematically off by a predictable factor, so HLL multiplies by a correction constant (α_m, depending on bucket count). At very small cardinalities it switches to a different method (linear counting), because the leading-zeros trick is unreliable when barely anything has been seen.

05The accuracy / memory dial

Standard error ≈ 1.04 / √m, where m is the bucket count. More buckets, more accuracy — a smooth trade. With m = 16,384, error ≈ 1.04/128 ≈ 0.8%. Each bucket stores only a small integer (the max leading-zero count never exceeds ~50, so 6 bits suffice): 16,384 × 6 bits ≈ 12 KB total, whether you're counting a thousand items or ten billion. That flat footprint is the entire point.

06The superpower — mergeability

Two HyperLogLog sketches can be merged into one representing the union of both streams by taking the element-wise maximum of their registers — bucket by bucket, keep the larger value. No re-scanning the original data.

So you can count distinct items across a whole fleet: each server keeps its own HLL over local traffic, and at the end you merge them all with bucket-wise max to get the cluster-wide distinct count — having shipped only ~12 KB per server instead of raw data. It's the same "small mergeable summary" theme as Merkle trees and Bloom-filter key summaries.

07Key terminology

Cardinality
The count of distinct elements — the quantity HLL estimates. Why it matters: it's a different question from membership (Bloom) or frequency — "how many uniques," not "is X here" or "how often X."
Register (bucket)
One of the m small counters, each holding the max leading-zero count for the items whose hash prefix routes to it. Why it matters: many registers = many independent estimators, which is what tames the huge variance of a single one.
Leading-zero count (rank ρ)
The position of the leftmost 1-bit in a hash's tail — the "rare pattern" signal. Why it matters: a max of k across items implies ~2^k distinct items; it's the raw estimator the whole method rests on.
Harmonic mean
The averaging method HLL uses to combine registers, chosen because it suppresses large outliers. Why it matters: it's the "Hyper" upgrade over LogLog's plain average — the single change that made the estimate accurate.
Standard error (1.04/√m)
The accuracy as a function of bucket count m. Why it matters: it's the exact dial — pick your error target, and it tells you how many buckets (hence how much memory) you need.
Mergeability
Two sketches combine by element-wise max of registers, yielding the union's cardinality. Why it matters: it makes HLL distributed-friendly — count across a cluster by shipping tiny sketches, not data.

08Where it's used

SystemHow it uses the idea
RedisPFADD / PFCOUNT / PFMERGE — the "PF" honors Philippe Flajolet, HLL's inventor. ~12 KB per key.
Presto / Trino, BigQueryAPPROX_DISTINCT / approximate COUNT(DISTINCT) over huge tables without the memory of exact counting.
Redshift / SnowflakeApproximate distinct-count functions for analytics at scale.
Network & analyticsUnique-IP / unique-user counting over firehose streams, and cluster-wide merges of per-node sketches.

09Common confusions

It counts distinct items, not volume or frequency. "How many unique visitors" — yes. "How many times did visitor A come" — it has no idea.
It is not a membership structure. Unlike a Bloom filter, it can't tell you whether a specific item was seen — only the count of distinct items. Bloom = "is X in the set?"; HLL = "how big is the set?"
You can't recover the elements. It keeps summary registers, not items — nothing to list or read back.
It's approximate by design. Need the exact distinct count? Use a real hash set and pay the memory. HLL is for when ~1% error is fine and memory matters.
Weakest at tiny cardinalities. The leading-zeros trick misbehaves when little has been seen — real implementations switch to linear counting at the low end.

10One-sentence summary

HyperLogLog estimates distinct-item counts in tiny fixed memory by hashing each item, tracking the maximum leading-zero count across many buckets, and fusing them with a bias-corrected harmonic mean — turning "the rarest pattern I've seen implies how many things I've seen" into a mergeable, ~1%-accurate cardinality counter.
